title: Six SNAP households the top three models deny
paragraphs: {eligibleCount} of the 100 households qualify for SNAP in the PolicyEngine reference. The top three models on the board, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1, and Kimi K3, each predict $0 for the same {deniedCount}: {deniedScenarios}. The reference for each is ${referenceAnnual} for the year, the minimum allotment (8% of the one-person maximum, ${referenceMonthly} a month, for households of one or two).

Five of the six qualify through broad-based categorical eligibility: Connecticut, Michigan, Texas, and Wisconsin confer SNAP eligibility on households receiving a TANF-funded non-cash benefit, with gross-income limits of 200% of poverty (CT, MI, WI) and 165% (TX) and the net-income and asset tests waived. The sixth, scenario_112 in Texas, passes the federal tests; the models counted farm-rent income the rules exclude.

{categoricalOnlyCount} of the {eligibleCount} eligible households qualify only through categorical eligibility: {categoricalIncomeCount} because income exceeds the federal limits, {categoricalAssetCount} because savings exceed the federal asset limit. On the {categoricalAssetCount} asset cases the models compute benefits near the reference: Sol within 1% on three and 10% on one, Fable 5.1 within 1% on all four.

In their SNAP explanations across the 100 households, Sol mentions categorical eligibility {solCategoricalMentions} time(s) and assets {solAssetMentions} times; Fable 5.1 mentions broad-based categorical eligibility {fableBbceMentions} times; Kimi K3 mentions categorical eligibility {kimiCategoricalMentions} times.

Pathways were recomputed with policyengine-us {pathwayEngineVersion} from the frozen scenarios and agree with the frozen reference SNAP values for all 100 households; the reference itself was generated with policyengine-us {referenceEngineVersion}.
